title: Rajnath Singh reviews LAC roads and new equipment at Army's Sukna base near Siliguri
dek: The defence minister was briefed on border infrastructure and the deployment of advanced weapons by the corps that guards the Sikkim frontier with China, and told troops modern warfare now includes drones and disinformation.
body:
Defence Minister Rajnath Singh reviewed the operational readiness of the Indian Army's Trishakti Corps at Sukna, near Siliguri in north Bengal, on Saturday, and was briefed on the building of infrastructure along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) with China and on the deployment of advanced military equipment and new technologies, the Ministry of Defence said.

The Chief of the Army Staff, General Dhiraj Seth, the head of the Army's Eastern Command, Lieutenant General VMB Krishnan, and the commander of 33 Corps, as the Trishakti Corps is formally known, Lieutenant General Man Raj Singh Mann, were present, according to the ministry's release. Mr Singh "expressed satisfaction" with the corps' preparedness and praised its work on roads and community welfare in border areas, the release said.

## What the minister said

Addressing soldiers at a barakhana, a shared meal, on the eve of Diwali, Mr Singh described Sukna as a critical hub for moving weapons, supplies, food, medical stores and troops to forward posts. "Sukna serves as a vital link in the security architecture of Eastern India," he said, according to the ministry.

He said the nature of war was changing. "Modern warfare extends beyond conventional battles," he said, listing hybrid warfare, proxy wars, cyber-attacks, drone incursions and information warfare, and said adversaries were using social media to spread rumours and drones to watch sensitive sites. "Defence Forces must remain vigilant," he said. He said Indian start-ups and companies were now making drones and anti-drone systems, and that spending on roads, tunnels, border infrastructure and modern equipment had risen under the government's self-reliance (Aatmanirbhar Bharat) policy. He did not give figures.

Mr Singh also spoke of the troops' morale and mental health, and repeated the government's description of the North-East as India's "first edge" rather than its last, according to the release. The ministry did not say which new systems had been deployed or where.

## Why Sukna matters

The Trishakti Corps, headquartered at Sukna in Darjeeling district, is responsible for the Sikkim stretch of the frontier with China and for the defence of the Siliguri Corridor, the strip of Indian land between Nepal and Bangladesh, only about 20 km wide at its narrowest, that links the North-East to the rest of the country. Bhutan lies to its north, and beyond it Tibet's Chumbi Valley, where China has expanded roads and military facilities in recent years.

The area was at the centre of the 2017 stand-off at Doklam, a plateau claimed by both Bhutan and China, where Indian troops blocked Chinese road construction for more than two months. Since the deadly clash in eastern Ladakh's Galwan valley in June 2020, both India and China have stepped up construction of roads, bridges, tunnels, airfields and shelters along the whole LAC. In October 2024 the two sides agreed on patrolling arrangements at the last friction points in Ladakh, but both still keep large forces on the frontier and the boundary remains undefined.

The visit came as the military pushes ahead with frontier logistics elsewhere: on Saturday the Indian Air Force reported a record landing of an IL-76 heavy transport aircraft at Nyoma in Ladakh, 25 km from the LAC.

## What it means

For Bengal, the corps' work is not only military: roads and bridges through the Darjeeling and Kalimpong hills into Sikkim also carry civilian traffic, tourists and trade. The minister's emphasis on drones and disinformation reflects a wider shift in how the Army describes threats on this frontier, beyond the troop build-ups of recent years. China's foreign ministry had not commented on the visit by Saturday night. Beijing has in the past objected to Indian leaders' visits to areas it claims, such as Arunachal Pradesh, but Sukna lies well inside undisputed Indian territory.
